category.text: $course$/Game Theory/Chapter 04 - Mixed Strategies and Nash's Existence Theorem (Quiz)

questiontext.text: When solving for a mixed Nash equilibrium of a 2x2 game, a player's mixing probabilities are chosen so that:

generalfeedback.text: Each player's probabilities make the opponent indifferent. If they did not, the opponent would have a strictly better reply and would shift all weight onto it, breaking the equilibrium. Your own indifference is a consequence of the opponent's choice of probabilities, not something you engineer.

answer.text: The opponent is indifferent between their pure strategies
The player maximises their own expected payoff over probabilities

feedback.text: Expected payoff is linear in one's own probability, so this alone does not pin an interior mix.

answer.text: Both players receive the same expected payoff
The variance of the player's payoff is minimised

feedback.text: Risk attitudes are already inside the payoff numbers.

questiontext.text: In Matching Pennies (payoffs \(+1\) to the matcher, \(-1\) to the mismatcher), with what probability does each player choose Heads in the unique Nash equilibrium? Give a decimal.

generalfeedback.text: Setting player 2's payoff from Heads equal to that from Tails gives \(1 - 2p = 2p - 1\), hence \(p = 0.5\). By symmetry both mix half and half, and each earns an expected \(0\).

name.text: C04 Q3 - Battle of the Sexes, Alex's mix

questiontext.text: In Battle of the Sexes with payoffs \((\text{Opera},\text{Opera}) = (2,1)\), \((\text{Football},\text{Football}) = (1,2)\) and \((0,0)\) off the diagonal, what probability does Alex place on Opera in the mixed equilibrium? Give a decimal to two places.

generalfeedback.text: Alex's probability \(p\) is set to make Bailey indifferent: Bailey gets \(p\) from Opera and \(2(1-p)\) from Football, so \(p = 2 - 2p\) and \(p = \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.67\). Symmetrically Bailey plays Opera with probability \(\tfrac{1}{3}\).

questiontext.text: How many Nash equilibria in total (pure and mixed) does Battle of the Sexes have?

generalfeedback.text: Three: the two pure equilibria (Opera, Opera) and (Football, Football), plus the mixed one at \(p = \tfrac{2}{3}\), \(q = \tfrac{1}{3}\). A classical result says almost every finite game has an odd number of equilibria, which is a useful sanity check on your count.

name.text: C04 Q5 - What Nash's theorem guarantees

questiontext.text: Nash's theorem states that every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium. Which qualification is essential?

generalfeedback.text: Existence is guaranteed only once mixed strategies are allowed. Matching Pennies has no pure equilibrium, so the theorem would simply be false for pure strategies. Mixing is what makes the best-response correspondence convex-valued and lets Kakutani's theorem apply.

answer.text: The equilibrium may require mixed strategies
The equilibrium can be computed in polynomial time

feedback.text: The problem is PPAD-complete; no such algorithm is known.

name.text: C04 Q6 - Payoff in the support

questiontext.text: If a player mixes between three pure strategies with positive probability in equilibrium, all three must give the same expected payoff against the opponents' strategies.

generalfeedback.text: True - this is the indifference principle. If one strategy in the support paid strictly more, moving all the probability onto it would raise the player's expected payoff, contradicting equilibrium. Strategies outside the support must pay no more than those inside.

questiontext.text: Which reading of a mixed equilibrium does not require any player to literally use a randomising device?

generalfeedback.text: Both the population reading (a fraction of a large population plays each pure strategy) and Harsanyi's purification (small private payoff shocks make each individual's behaviour pure, while others see a distribution) avoid literal randomisation. Harsanyi's argument is the standard defence of mixed equilibria against the charge of implausibility.

answer.text: The population interpretation, and Harsanyi's purification via small private payoff shocks

feedback.text: That one is precisely about using a device.
That is a computational condition, not an interpretation.
That describes the existence proof, not behaviour.

name.text: C04 Q8 - Expected payoff against a mixture

questiontext.text: Player 1's payoffs from strategy \(A\) are \(6\) against \(L\) and \(0\) against \(R\). Player 2 plays \(L\) with probability \(0.25\) and \(R\) with probability \(0.75\). What is player 1's expected payoff from \(A\)?

generalfeedback.text: \(u_1(A, \sigma_2) = 0.25 \times 6 + 0.75 \times 0 = 1.5\). Expected payoff is always linear in the opponent's probabilities, which is exactly why a player who is not indifferent would shift all weight to one side.
